{{Short description|Minimum number of times a specific knot must be passed through itself to become untied}}
[[Image:Unknotting trefoil.svg|300px|thumb|Trefoil knot without 3-fold symmetry being unknotted by one crossing switch.]]
[[File:Unknotting Whitehead link.svg|thumb|[[Whitehead link]] being unknotted by undoing one crossing]]

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] area of [[knot theory]], the '''unknotting number''' of a [[knot (mathematics)|knot]] is the minimum number of times the knot must be passed through itself ('''crossing switch''') to untie it. If a knot has unknotting number <math>n</math>, then there exists a [[knot diagram|diagram]] of the knot which can be changed to [[unknot]] by switching <math>n</math> crossings.<ref>{{cite book |author=Adams, Colin Conrad |title=The knot book: an elementary introduction to the mathematical theory of knots |publisher=American Mathematical Society |location=Providence, Rhode Island |year=2004 |pages=56 |isbn=0-8218-3678-1}}</ref> The unknotting number of a knot is always less than half of its [[crossing number (knot theory)|crossing number]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Taniyama | first = Kouki
 | doi = 10.1142/S0218216509007361
 | issue = 8
 | journal = Journal of Knot Theory and Its Ramifications
 | mr = 2554334
 | pages = 1049–1063
 | title = Unknotting numbers of diagrams of a given nontrivial knot are unbounded
 | volume = 18
 | year = 2009| arxiv = 0805.3174
 }}.</ref> This [[knot invariant|invariant]] was first defined by Hilmar Wendt in 1936.<ref name="Wendt1937">{{cite journal
 |last1=Wendt
 |first1=Hilmar
 |title=Die gordische Auflösung von Knoten
 |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift
 |date=December 1937
 |volume=42
 |issue=1
 |pages=680–696
 |doi=10.1007/BF01160103}}</ref>

Any [[composite knot]] has unknotting number at least two, and therefore every knot with unknotting number one is a [[prime knot]]. The unknotting number is not additive under [[connected sum]],<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Brittenham |first1=Mark |last2=Hermiller |first2=Susan |title=Unknotting number is not additive under connected sum |eprint=2506.24088 |class=math.GT |year=2025}}</ref> although that possibility, implicit in [Wendt,1937<ref name="Wendt1937"/>] and explicitly asked by Gordon in 1977<ref name="GordonAspects">{{cite book | last=Gordon | first=C. M. | editor-last=Hausmann | editor-first=Jean-Claude | title=Knot Theory | chapter=Some aspects of classical knot theory | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | publication-place=Berlin, Heidelberg | volume=685 | date=1978 | isbn=978-3-540-08952-0 | doi=10.1007/bfb0062968 | url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BFb0062968 | access-date=2025-09-14 | mr=521730 | page=1–60}}This volume is dedicated to the memory of Christos Demetriou Papakyriakopoulos, 1914–1976.</ref> and many others, was not resolved until 2025. A counterexample showed that the unknotting number of the connected sum of [[71 knot|7<sub>1</sub>]] and its mirror image was at most 5, one less than the sum of the numbers from its components.<ref name="QuantaUnknotting">{{cite web | last=Sloman | first=Leila | title=A Simple Way To Measure Knots Has Come Unraveled | website=Quanta Magazine | date=2025-09-22 | url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-simple-way-to-measure-knots-has-come-unraveled-20250922/ | access-date=2025-09-22}}</ref>

In general, it is relatively difficult to determine the unknotting number of a given knot. Known cases include:
* The unknotting number of a nontrivial [[twist knot]] is always equal to one.
* The unknotting number of a <math>(p,q)</math>-[[torus knot]] is equal to <math>(p-1)(q-1)/2</math>.<ref>{{MathWorld|id=TorusKnot|title=Torus Knot}}<math>\frac{1}{2}(p-1)(q-1)</math>".</ref>
* The unknotting numbers of [[prime knot]]s with nine or fewer [[crossing number (knot theory)|crossings]] have all been determined.<ref>{{MathWorld|title=Unknotting Number|urlname=UnknottingNumber}}</ref> (The unknotting number of the 10<sub>11</sub> prime knot is unknown.)
